## Why organizational action measures matter

Actions taken to support the use of open data indicate organizational commitment to transparency and share what data is collected and being used to provide public services and inform government response to community issues.

## Dataset and Data Product Measures

New datasets often represent the fulfillment of public requests [@mergel2018] or commitment of departments and programs to publish data that shows how their work serves the public [@johnson2016]. Government response to public health emergencies, severe weather events, and local issues can be measured in part by the new applications and websites created to provide information and connect people to needed services.

The Information Services team at Baton Rouge created a map application to inform and guide their response to a major flood event [@koma2016]. They also invited the public to contact their department directly to update them about property damage [@gallo2016]. The flood inundation map continues to rank as one of the top data products accessed by the public [@cityofbatonrougeandparishofeastbatonrougeb].

Senate bills passed by the state authorizing immigration checks by public safety departments led to the city council in Austin to pass a resolution directing the Police Department to end most arrests for citation-eligible offenses and to provide detailed data about discretionary arrests for leadership review [@wilson2018a; @cityofaustin2018a]. The publishing of the Immigration Status Dataset and Guide [@cityofaustintexas-austinpolice; @cityofaustina] to the open data portal enabled both internal and external reviews of arrests and racial disparities [@sanders2020; @gates2020; @cronk2020].

By providing the context of new dataset and data products, organizations can demonstrate how open data supports the priorities of local government and the public.

## Support Measures

Content created to train users on how to use open data and data products demonstrate program commitment to the public. Dedicated communication channels for technical support or to ask data owners questions demonstrate accountability for the systems and data published on data portals.

## Event Measures

Open data day celebrations, datathons, and hackathons are ways that open data programs, departments, community organizations, researchers, local news organizations, and technology sponsors typically engage the public to participate in a day, weekend, or week of using government data to help understand and tackle important community issues. The number of events hosted and supported are measures that demonstrate program engagement with the public.

## Organization Change Measures

Additions to staffing or changes to groups to ensure there is adequate staff to publish new data, address increases in data work, and facilitate coordination show commitment to making data publicly available.

An example of an organization change in Baton Rouge made to improve analytics capacity is the integration of the GIS staff with the Information Services team to form a unified Division of Data, Analytics and Performance team and the creation of a dedicated outreach coordinator position [@cityofbatonrougeandparishofeastbatonrouge2023a].

## Data Collection

The number of new datasets and some data products may be found from the catalogs provided by data portals and filtered by creation date and asset type. Context may also be available for those assets if that information has been added to the description, category, data owner, and other metadata fields. New applications and websites that are created outside of a data portal will require manual collection but likely will be tracked by an internal system used for department and technical support teams.

Events may be manually tracked by departments spreadsheets or available through event registration software.

New and updated systems that provide support and facilitate communication may be tracked through internal project portfolio systems.

## Reporting

Reporting organizational actions should include narrative that describes the context and motivations for the actions. Ongoing reporting may show lifetime values of actions and results. Annual reporting provides a snapshot for the program, enabling tracking of progress over time.

A consistent feature of the Baton Rouge annual open data policy report is the "By the Numbers" section that shows both the number of datasets, data products, events, and engagements, as well as the resulting social media impressions and views of data assets and support videos [@cityofbatonrougeandparishofeastbatonrouge2025b].
